90-015.r: Indian Independence Bill: introduced in House of Commons by Attlee July 4, 1947; passed Commons July 15, Lords next day; Royal Assent July 18th, 1947.

90-016.r: 'Plan Balkan' for fragmentation of India → Lord Mountbatten's brainchild: separate dominions for Pakistan, the Princely States and the rest.

90-017.r: Congress agreed to partition in 1947 mainly to avoid large-scale communal riots; Mountbatten announced partition plan on 3rd June 1947 amid communal violence.

90-018.r: Congress accepted Mountbatten Plan (A true) to avoid communal riots, but never accepted Two-Nation Theory (R false).

90-019.r: Gandhi's alternative to partition (first meeting with Mountbatten, 31st March 1947) → ask Jinnah to become Prime Minister of Interim Government; Congress leaders rejected it.

90-020.r: Radcliffe Committee → demarcate India-Pakistan boundary; Mountbatten formed Punjab and Bengal Border Commissions (June 30, 1947), both headed by Cyril Radcliffe.

90-022.r: Both Boundary Commissions (Bengal, Punjab) of 1947 headed by British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe; Radcliffe Award published 17 August 1947, two days after partition.

90-023.r: Last chance to avoid partition lost with rejection of Cabinet Mission plan (16 May 1946): League accepted it 6th June 1946, rejected it July 29, called for 'Direct Action'.

90-024.r: Congress accepted partition resolution at Delhi, 14/15 June 1947 → President J.B. Kripalani; proposal moved by Gobind Ballabh Pant, supported by Azad, Patel, Nehru.

90-026.r: AICC, New Delhi, 14-15 June 1947 (approving 3rd June plan): partition resolution moved by Gobind Vallabh Pant, seconded by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.

90-027.r: Partition resolution = 'Surrender of nationalism in favour of communalism' → Dr. Kitchlew, Punjab Congress president; he later joined Communist Party of India.

90-028.r: AICC Delhi, June 14-15, 1947: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Frontier/Seemant Gandhi) voted against partition.

90-029.r: Constituent Assembly, as Provisional Parliament, assumed sovereign power at midnight 14-15 August 1947; Nehru spoke there as first Prime Minister.

90-030.r: Central Assembly, midnight 14/15 August 1947: Sucheta Kriplani sang 'Jan-Gan-Man' and Iqbal's 'Sare Jahan Se Achha Hindustan Hamara'.

90-031.r: First Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru was appointed by the Governor-General, Lord Mountbatten.

90-032.r: First Governor-General of independent India → Lord Mountbatten (1947-48); first Indian Governor-General → C. Rajagopalachari (1948-50).
90-032.t: Don't confuse first Governor-General (Mountbatten) with first Indian Governor-General (Rajagopalachari).

90-034.r: C. Rajagopalachari (1948-50) → last Governor-General, and the first and last Indian one; later Chief Minister of Madras (1952-54); formed Swatantra Party 1959.
90-034.h: Rajaji closes the Governor-General era: first Indian, last ever.

90-037.r: Last Viceroy → Lord Mountbatten (1947-48); took charge 24 March 1947; presented partition plan June 3, 1947.

90-038.r: First Law Minister of independent India → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (on Gandhi's recommendation); also chaired Constitution's Drafting Committee.

90-039.r: First four Presidents of India: Rajendra Prasad (1950-1962), S. Radhakrishnan (1962-1967), Zakir Hussain (1967-1969), V.V. Giri (1969-1974).

90-040.r: Partition Council under Lord Mountbatten → Congress represented by Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Patel; plan presented June 3, 1947.

90-041.r: Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947): Punjab and Bengal assemblies vote on partition in Hindu and Muslim groups; referendum in NWFP, Sindh, Baluchistan, Sylhet (Assam).

90-042.r: Congress President at partition and on 15th August 1947 → J.B. Kripalani (Meerut session 1946; 23rd November 1946 to November 1947); then Rajendra Prasad.

90-046.r: Mahatma Gandhi joined no Independence Day celebration on 15 August 1947; saddened by partition, he fasted and prayed.

90-047.r: Constitution enforced 26 January 1950 because Congress had celebrated 26 January 1930 as first Independence Day (Purna Swaraj goal, Lahore session 1929).

90-048.r: 'Indian Nationalism was the child of the British Rule' → R. Coupland.

90-049.r: 'Most notable achievement of British Rule was the unification of India' → K.M. Panikkar.

90-050.r: British Monarch at Indian Independence → George VI (King of UK 1936-1952).

90-051.r: Saurashtra Sangh formed 15th February 1948 by merging 222 principalities (217 of Kathiawar Agency + 5 others).

91-001.r: Regulating Act 1773 → first post of Governor-General of (Fort William in) Bengal, supervising Madras and Bombay Presidencies; Council of four.

91-005.r: Regulating Act 1773 → first Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (functioning 1774): Chief Justice + three judges; first Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey.

91-008.r: Act of 1786 → Governor-General (Cornwallis) could override his Council's majority in special cases (peace, defence, welfare); Cornwallis wanted also Commander-in-Chief powers.

91-010.r: 1793 (Cornwallis Code): District Collector lost judicial powers, became only revenue collector → Cornwallis feared absolute power in one person (separation of powers).

91-011.r: Charter Act 1813 → ended East India Company's monopoly of Indian trade, except tea and trade with China.
91-011.t: Don't confuse: 1813 kept tea and China monopoly; 1833 ended the Company's trade entirely.

91-015.r: Charter Act 1813 → Company made responsible for Indians' education; annual grant of 1 lakh rupees for education.

91-016.r: Charter Act 1833: Company's trade (China, tea) ended; Governor-General of Bengal → Governor-General of India; all law-making powers to him in Council. Not: an Indian Law Member.

91-018.r: Simultaneous ICS exam in India and England → recommended by Montagu-Chelmsford Report; held from 1922; Aitchison Commission (1887) had opposed it.

91-019.r: Charter Act 1853 → competitive exam for Civil Services (Directors lost patronage); Directors cut from 24 to 18, 6 nominated by Crown.

91-020.r: Charter Act of 1853 → first functioning Legislative Council in India (12 members); separated executive and legislative powers.

91-021.r: ICS exam held simultaneously in India and England from 1922; Lee Commission (1924) → Public Service Commission set up 1926.

91-022.r: Government of India Act 1919 → ICS exam also in India (from 1922); by 1st January 1941 Indians (617) outnumbered Europeans (585) in ICS.

91-023.r: Board of Control → Pitt's India Act 1784; Supreme Court → Regulating Act 1773; Christian missionaries allowed → Charter Act 1813; Law Member in Governor-General's Council → Charter Act 1833.

91-024.r: Charter Act 1813 → trade monopoly ended; Regulating Act 1773 → directors show correspondence to Government; Act of 1858 → Crown rule; Pitt's India Act 1784 → Board of Control.

91-026.r: Flawed question: MPPSC treated it as wrong and gave bonus marks. Book: had it said 'sugar and China', answer would be Charter Act 1833.
91-026.c: No answer printed; question deleted by MPPSC. Book's 'sugar and China' remark is itself unclear.

91-027.r: Company lost tea trade monopoly → Charter Act 1833, which ended all its commercial rights; Company kept only administration for the Crown.
91-027.t: Don't pick 1813: it ended general trade monopoly but kept tea.

91-028.r: 1834: almost all of present Uttar Pradesh separated from Bengal Presidency → North-Western Provinces under Agra Presidency.

91-029.r: Government of India Act 1858 → rule passed from East India Company to Crown; Secretary of State for India with 15-member Council of India (8 Crown, 7 Directors).

91-030.r: Company's Indian trade monopoly ended by Charter Act 1813, not 1853 (statement 1 false); Government of India Act 1858 → Crown ruled India directly (true).

91-031.r: Indian Councils Act 1861 → Governor-General could issue Ordinances in emergency, valid for maximum 6 months.

91-032.r: Indian Councils Act 1861 → strengthened Viceroy; Canning brought 'portfolio' (departmental) system, each department under one member, replacing corporate functioning.

91-033.r: Indian Councils Act 1892 → members could discuss budget and ask questions on budget and public matters; no supplementary questions.

91-034.r: Indian Councils Act of 1892 → first introduced principle of representation and indirect elections.

91-035.r: Acts to control press: Press Act 1835; Press and Registration of Books Act 1867; Vernacular Press Act 1878 (Lytton); Lord Minto's Act 1908.

91-036.r: High Courts of Bombay, Madras, Calcutta → under Indian High Courts Act 1861 (set up 1862).

91-037.r: Most short-lived constitutional experiment → Indian Councils Act 1909; Ramsay MacDonald: incomplete, short-term agreement between democracy and bureaucracy.

91-038.r: Communal representation → Minto-Morley Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909); Lord Minto = 'Father of Communal Electorate'.

91-039.r: Separate electorate (for Muslims) introduced by Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms).

91-040.r: Reform declaration of 20th August 1917 → 'Montagu Declaration', by Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State for India) with Lord Chelmsford.

91-041.r: Father of Dyarchy → Sir Lionel Curtis; Dyarchy = double government in provinces under Government of India Act (1919).

91-042.r: Montagu-Chelmsford Report (Secretary of State Edwin Montagu + Viceroy Lord Chelmsford) → basis of Government of India Act, 1919.

91-043.r: UK Prime Minister when Montagu-Chelmsford Act passed (1919) → David Lloyd George (PM 1916 to 1922).

91-044.r: Dyarchy in provinces → Government of India Act 1919: provincial subjects split into Reserved (finance, law and order, police) and Transferred (health, education, agriculture, local self-government).
91-044.h: Reserved = with Governor; Transferred = to Indian ministers.

91-050.r: Government of India Act 1919: governance did not stay unitary and central (A false); large authority delegated to provinces (R true): 50 subjects provincial, 47 central.

91-051.r: Dyarchy (Act of 1919) = provincial subjects split into Reserved and Transferred; introduced to bring responsible government in provinces; A and R true, R explains A.

91-052.r: Post of Indian High Commissioner → created by Government of India Act, 1919.

91-053.r: Government of India Act 1935 → Federation, Provincial Autonomy, Federal Legislature, bicameral legislatures; abolished dyarchy in provinces (so dyarchy not its element).
91-053.c: Explanation says the Act provided a Federal Legislature (statement 4), yet the answer is only 1 and 2; no option offers 1, 2 and 4.

91-055.r: Baseline of Government of India Act 1935 → Simon Commission (1927), set up under 1919 Act's 10-year review clause; plus Nehru Report and Round Table Conferences.

91-056.r: Government of India Act 1935 (passed August 1935): abolished dyarchy in provinces; Governors could veto and legislate themselves. Did not abolish communal representation.

91-058.r: Government of India Act 1935: reconstructed Governor-General's Executive Council, Provincial Autonomy, proposed Federation; main source of Indian Constitution. Not: dyarchy in both Centre and provinces.

91-062.r: 1935 Act put Princely States in Federation → to use princes to counter-balance nationalists; States had ~25% population but 104 of 260 seats (provinces 156).

91-063.r: Government of India Act 1935 = 'a car (machine) with strong brakes but no engine' → Jawaharlal Nehru.

91-065.r: 'Principle of Constitutional Autocracy' → Government of India Act 1935, most elaborate British Act; set up federation, federal judiciary, Centre-state division of powers.

91-066.r: Congress rejected Government of India Act 1935 at Lucknow Session 1936, presided by Jawaharlal Nehru.

91-067.r: Central Legislative Assembly elections under 1919 Act → 1923, 1926, 1930, 1934, 1945 (last); 1937 provincial elections were under 1935 Act.

91-069.r: Government of India Act 1935 = 'Charter of Slavery' → Jawaharlal Nehru; Royal Assent 2 August 1935; 14 Parts, 321 Sections, 10 Schedules.
91-069.h: Nehru's two jibes at 1935 Act: 'Charter of Slavery' and 'all brakes, no engine'.

91-070.r: 'Instrument of Instructions' in Government of India Act 1935 → became Directive Principles of State Policy in Constitution (1950).
hi: Directive Principles of State Policy (राज्य के नीति निदेशक तत्व)

91-071.r: Federation under Government of India Act 1935 → residuary powers with the Governor General.
91-071.t: Don't pick Federal Legislature: in the 1935 Act residuary powers went to the Governor General.

91-072.r: India Council abolished by Government of India Act 1935; Act ended dyarchy in provinces and started it at Centre; more provincial autonomy.

91-073.r: 'I have not to beg pardon... major part of Government of India Act, 1935 reproduced' in draft Constitution → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

91-074.r: 'Can you show me one free country where there are separate electorates?... British left mischief behind' → Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel, Constituent Assembly debates.

91-075.r: Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court; Indian Councils Act 1909 → Communal Electorate; Government of India Act 1919 → Dyarchy; Government of India Act 1935 → Provincial Autonomy.

91-076.r: Not a British-era constitutional landmark → Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (earlier Untouchability (Offences) Act; notified 8th May 1955; renamed 1976; punishes untouchability).

92-001.r: Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court at Calcutta (true); Indian Penal Code 1860 (true); first regular British-pattern police → Cornwallis, not Warren Hastings (false).

92-002.r: 19th-century Anglo-Afghan relations → British fear of Russian expansion towards India (after Russia-Iran Treaty of Turkmenchay, 1828); feared invasion via Khyber and Bolan Passes.

92-003.r: 1775 → First Anglo-Maratha War; 1780 → Second Anglo-Mysore War; 1824 → First Anglo-Burmese War; 1838 → First Anglo-Afghan War (declared 1838, fought 1839-1842).

92-004.r: Second Anglo-Mysore War 1780-84; Second Anglo-French War 1750-54 (1749-54); Second Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05; Second Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80.

92-005.r: Treaty of Allahabad 1765; Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle 1748; La Bourdannais captured Madras 1746; Dupleix dismissed 1754.

92-006.r: Order: Second Anglo-French (Carnatic) War 1749-1754 → First Anglo-Mysore 1767-1769 → First Anglo-Afghan 1839-1842 → First Anglo-Sikh 1845-1846.

92-007.r: Farrukhsiyar → re-imposed Jizya; Colonel Francis Ford → took Masulipatnam (1759); William Bentinck → Bengal Sati Regulation 1829; Malcolm → not linked with end of slavery.
92-007.c: The book gives no single answer (*): its explanation faults two options, (d) Malcolm is not linked with ending slavery, and (c) should name the Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829.

92-008.r: 'Paternalism in Governance' → Sir Thomas Munro (1761-1827); also John Malcolm, Elphinstone, Charles Metcalfe.

92-009.r: 'Sea of Calamity' → Orissa Famine of 1866-67; about 13 lakh (1.3 million) people, a third of Odisha's population, died.

92-010.r: Indian Famine Code, 1883 → prepared by Strachey Commission (appointed 1878 after Great Famine of 1876-78).

92-011.r: Famine commissions: Campbell (1866, Orissa famine), Lyall (after 1896-97 famine), Strachey. Not Hunter Commission.

92-012.r: Andrew Frazer → Police Commission (1902-03); Antony MacDonell → Famine (1900-01); Colin Scott Moncrieff → Irrigation (1901-03); Thomas Robertson → Railway (1901-03).

92-013.r: Correct: 1790-92 → Third Mysore War; 1824-26 → First Anglo-Burmese War. Wrong: First Anglo-Maratha War was 1775-82, not 1767-69; 1845-46 was First, not Second, Sikh War.

92-014.r: Order: Nana Phadnavis died (March 1800) → Wellesley recalled → Vellore Mutiny (July 10, 1806, Tamil Nadu) → Anglo-Nepalese War.

92-015.r: Order: Battle of Wandiwash (1760, Third Carnatic War) → Raja Nand Kumar hanged (1775, forgery, Calcutta) → Treaty of Salbai (1782) → Death of Tipu Sultan.

92-016.r: Order: Battle of Shakarkheda (1724) → Bedara (1759) → Porto Novo (1781) → Mudki (1845).

92-017.r: Latest of these → Moplah Revolt (1921, Mappila Muslims of Malabar); Home Rule began April 1916; Khilafat Movement 1919-24 (Ali brothers, backed by Gandhi).

92-018.r: Queen Elizabeth II → reigned 70 years (1952-2022), died aged 96 (born 1926).

92-019.r: Order: Dramatic Performances Act 1876 → Vernacular Press Act 1878 → Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 → North-Western Provinces and Oudh Act 1890.

92-020.r: Child marriage → M.G. Ranade; suppression of Thuggee → Colonel Sleimen (Sleeman); widow remarriage → Ishwarchand Vidyasagar; suppression of Pindaris → Lord Hastings.

92-021.r: 1857: Kunwar Singh → Bihar; Khan Bahadur Khan → Rohilkhand; Faizabad → Maulavi Ahmed Ullah, not Zeenat Mahal. Deliverance Day → 22 December 1939. Ghadar Party → 1913, Har Dayal.
92-021.c: No single answer (*): only statements 1 and 2 are correct, and no option gives that pair.

92-022.r: First Indian cinema advertisement → The Times of India, July 7th 1896; Lumiere brothers (France) gave first cinematograph show at Watson's Hotel, Bombay.

92-023.r: 'The British Government is not responsible for the partition of India' → Lord (Clement) Attlee, who on February 20, 1947 announced transfer of power to responsible Indians.

92-024.r: 'Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation' → Aurobindo Ghosh (political career about 1901 to 1910); claimed freedom as an inherent right, not due to misgovernment.

92-025.r: 'Party Less Democracy' in India → proposed by Jaya Prakash Narayan.

92-026.r: Rajani Palme Dutt: 'They both fought and collaborated with imperialism' → about the Indian National Congress.

92-027.r: 'New Lamps for Old' (1893-94), criticising Congress as out of touch with the proletariat → Aurobindo Ghose, in Bombay weekly 'Induprakash' (K.G. Deshpande's request).

92-028.r: Order: Hicky's Bengal Gazette 1780 → Bengal Asiatic Society (William Jones) 1784 → Servants of India Society (Gokhale) 1905 → Gadar Party (Lala Hardayal) 1913.

92-029.r: William A.J. Archibald (1865-1947): principal of M.A.O. College, Aligarh (1905 to 1909); helped organise Shimla Deputation 1906 to Lord Minto. Never principal of Lahore College.

92-030.r: 'I am an Indian Tom-Tom, whose work is waking up all the sleepers...' → Annie Besant.

92-031.r: 'So long as this third power, England, is here, communal differences would keep troubling us' → Mahatma Gandhi to Louis Fischer; so answer 'None of the above'.

92-032.r: Leaders who toured India widely for social regeneration → Gandhi and Tilak; Tilak, first national leader close to the public, was Gandhi's precursor.

92-033.r: Lala Lajpat Rai: first opposed Non-cooperation, later backed Gandhi (Calcutta special session, September 1920, under his presidency); also helped form Swaraj Party.

92-034.r: First Speaker to drop the official wig and wear Gandhi cap → G.V. Mavalankar (Central Legislative Assembly President, 1946); later first Lok Sabha Speaker.

92-035.r: World's first woman Prime Minister → Sirimavo Bhandaranaike of Sri Lanka (July 1960).

92-036.r: Official residence of British Prime Minister ('First Lord of the Treasury') → 10 Downing Street, Westminster.

92-037.r: Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party formed by J.B. Kripalani in 1951, not July 1952; P.C. Ghosh, T. Prakasam in it; merged with Socialist Party 1952 → Praja Socialist Party.

92-038.r: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: born April 14, 1891, Mhow (MP); died December 6, 1956, New Delhi; Bharat Ratna posthumously 1990.

92-039.r: 'Gurudev' → Rabindranath Tagore; first Asian Nobel laureate (1913, 'Song Offerings', English Gitanjali); knighted by George V; founded Visva Bharati.

92-040.r: Rabindranath Tagore: born May 7, 1861, Kolkata; died August 7, 1941 at ancestral home, Calcutta.
92-040.h: Tagore's dates both fall on the 7th: born 7 May, died 7 August.

92-041.r: 'The Great Sentinel' → Mahatma Gandhi's name for Rabindranath Tagore.
92-041.t: Don't mix titles: Gandhi called Tagore 'Great Sentinel'; Tagore called Subhas Bose 'Desh Nayak'.

92-042.r: Tagore did not favour economic aspects of Swadeshi Movement (showed side-effects in novel 'Ghare Baire'); praised ancient India; saw Shivaji, Guru Govind Singh as nation builders.

92-043.r: 'Avenge the blood of Indian Martyrs... Stand up against the entire Anglo-American enemy' → Ras Behari Bose, key organiser of INA.

92-044.r: 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan' → PM Lal Bahadur Shastri, 1965, Ramlila Maidan, New Delhi.

92-045.r: Present-day calendar used worldwide → Gregorian Calendar.

92-046.r: Bhartiya Kisan Sangh → founded 4th March 1979 at Kota, Rajasthan, by Dattopant Thengdi.
92-046.c: No answer printed; explanation gives 1979, which matches none of the options.

92-047.r: 'Freedom is almost within reach, we have to seize it' → Mahatma Gandhi, at the start of Quit India Movement, along with the slogan 'Do or Die'.

92-048.r: 'India's salvation will not be achieved under (Gandhi's) leadership' → Subhash Chandra Bose in his book 'The Indian Struggle'.

92-049.r: Early nationalists saw British rule as Providence bringing modernisation (A true); they complained only of 'Un-British rule' (R true); R does not explain A.

92-050.r: 'Everything else can wait, but not agriculture' → Jawaharlal Nehru, after Independence.

92-051.r: First successful cloth mill in Bombay → 1854, by Parsi merchant Cowaszee Nanabhoy Davar; first Indian cotton mill at Fort Gloster, Kolkata (1818) failed.

92-052.r: 'Kings are made for Public; Public is not made for the King' → Dadabhai Naoroji, Grand Old Man of India.

92-053.r: Boy Scouts and Guides Movement → Robert Baden-Powell; first camp at Brownsea Island, 1 August 1907 (20 boys); spread worldwide from 1908.

92-054.r: Rakhmabai case (1884-1888, child-bride marriage) → age of consent and restitution of conjugal rights, not education; led to Age of Consent Act 1891.

92-055.r: Untrue claim: 'Karachi Congress (1931) opposed Gandhi-Irwin Pact'. True: Rowlatt Act → Jallianwala Bagh; Bose → Forward Bloc; Bhagat Singh co-founded Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.

92-056.r: Nehru statements all false: 1947 Congress President → J.B. Kripalani; Constituent Assembly → Sachchidananda Sinha (interim), Rajendra Prasad (11th December 1946); not in first UP Congress ministry.

92-057.r: 'I am a socialist and a republican and am no believer in Kings and Princes' → Jawaharlal Nehru.

92-058.r: 'High priest of Communism in India' → Jawaharlal Nehru, so labelled in UP Publicity Department's propaganda pamphlet 'Communistic Likes and Dislikes'.

92-059.r: 1933: champion of socialism wanting to end British rule, princely states, landlordism, capitalism → Jawaharlal Nehru; influenced by Soviet socialism (visited November 1927).

92-060.r: Biographer of Jawaharlal Nehru → Frank Moraes.
92-060.t: Don't confuse with Louis Fischer, biographer of Mahatma Gandhi.

92-061.r: Ambabai → woman freedom fighter from Mysore state (Karnataka); young widow; picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops in Udipi during Salt Satyagraha.

92-062.r: Sarabandi (no-tax) campaign → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel at Bardoli (Surat, Gujarat), 1928; begun by Mehta brothers (Kalyanji, Kunwarji) and Dayalji Desai.
92-062.c: Question dates it to 1922; book itself says the year is wrong and gives 1928.

92-063.r: 'Boycott' named after Captain Charles C. Boycott, Irish land agent, first used as political weapon in 1880.

92-064.r: Labour representative to first ILO conference, Washington, 1919 → N.M. Joshi; B.P. Wadia went as his adviser.

92-065.r: Arya Samaj 1875 (Dayananda); 'Al Hilal' Urdu weekly by Abul Kalam Azad (1912); Hindu (Presidency) College 1817 → Ram Mohan Roy, David Hare; Lajpat Rai linked with 'The People'.

92-066.r: Order: 'Kesari' by Tilak 1881 → Khudiram Bose executed 1908 → Curzon Wyllie assassinated 1909 → 'Al Hilal' by Abul Kalam Azad 1912.

92-067.r: Order: Champaran 1917 → Non-Cooperation 1920-22 → Dandi March 1930 (third) → Quit India 1942.

92-068.r: Wrong pair: James Augustus Hicky – Calcutta Chronicle; he started 'Hicky's Bengal Gazette' (1780). Right: Dayananda – Satyarth Prakash; Ramaswamy Naicker – Justice Party; Phule – Satyashodhak Samaj.
